summary: Dense clipped hedge block with convincing leaf cards close up, but a perfect rounded box with one flat saturated green, no woody base and no growth variation.
critique: Read from a distance, this is a soft-cornered cuboid with leaves stuck on it. The front and back faces are almost planar and the top is flat with only small bald dents, so the silhouette from the side view is a capsule-ended slab. Real clipped hawthorn/privet/beech hedges are wider at the base than the top (a batter of roughly 10-15 cm per side), have an uneven top with sprigs of new growth poking 5-15 cm above the cut line, and thin out in the bottom 20-30 cm to show grey-brown stems, dead leaves and shadowed hollows. Here the leaves run right down to the turf with a dark ring. Colour is one mid-saturated yellow-green over the whole volume. There is no gradient from darker, older inner foliage to lighter fresh tips, no brown or yellowed patches and no sun/shade difference between the top and the sides. The dark 'holes' on the faces look like missing cards rather than depth. Leaf-card scale reads a little large for privet/box. Proportions (~1.5 m H x ~1 m W) are within the reference range for a clipped field hedge.
suggestions: Shape: give the core mesh a batter (bottom 1.1 m wide, top 0.85-0.9 m) and add low-frequency noise of +/-5-8 cm to the faces and top so the planes wave slightly. This costs nothing extra, because it only displaces the existing card anchors.

Base: stop the leaf cards 15-25 cm above the ground and fill the gap with 20-40 crossed stem cards (grey-brown, about 0.35 albedo, roughness 0.9). Add a 1-2 m strip of leaf-litter decal under the footprint. This adds roughly 150 triangles.
Top: scatter 30-60 single 'sprig' cards that stick 5-15 cm above the clipped top line and sides, so the outline is no longer a clean box.

Colour: tint cards by depth and height. Inner cards should be about 30% darker and bluer, outer tip cards lighter and yellower, plus 3-5% of cards brown or yellow. Encode this in vertex colour so there is no extra texture.

Cut the leaf-card scale by roughly 30% for a privet/box read, or switch to a hawthorn/beech atlas with mixed leaf sizes. Make sure the cards' normals point outward from the hedge core so the faces get soft shading, not per-card speckle.
Ends: let the square-cut end faces shade down to the stems, and break the rounded corners with a couple of over-long shoots.
renderer_notes: The uniform lawn and lack of AO/GI make the base contact look harsher than it would in an engine with SSAO. The missing translucency on leaf cards is a shader limitation.

summary: Correct 240 L wheelie bin layout (tapered body, hinged lid, front comb bar, rear axle and wheels) with good decals, but plastic surfaces are flat, boxy and too clean.
critique: The proportions match the 240 L reference (roughly 1.07 m H x 0.58 m W x 0.74 m D), and the part list is right: the hinge knuckles and handle bar at the rear, the lifting comb on the front, the axle and two wheels, the stepped lid and the stack lugs. The council label and stencilled '27' help a lot. Where it falls down: (1) The comb bar under the lid is a plain sharp-edged rectangular box. Real bins have a moulded U-channel with ribs and a continuous upper rim lip that wraps all four sides. (2) The body panels are flat with only faint vertical lines. A real bin has strong vertical stiffening ribs at the corners and a moulded recessed panel on each side, and the lower front often has a kick plate and feet. (3) The lid is too thin and flat on top, without the raised moulded handle at the front edge or the domed centre. (4) The wheels look small and thin (they should be about 200 mm in diameter and 50 mm wide with a chunky tread) and the axle housing is a box. (5) The material is a uniform dark grey-green with a slight sheen and almost no wear. Real bins have scuffing on the front lower edge and the lid lip, grime streaks from the lid down, faded and chalky UV-weathered tops, and a darker dirty base. The bottom of the body floats on a thin plate with a visible gap.
suggestions: Rebuild the front comb bar as a 3-sided U-channel (about 60 mm deep, 40 mm high) with a rounded bevel. Add a continuous 20-30 mm rim lip around the body top that the lid sits on. This adds roughly 200 triangles.

Add vertical corner ribs: two raised strips per corner, 15 mm proud. Add a shallow recessed panel (5-8 mm) on each side face. Add moulded feet at the front base so the bin sits on 4 contact points (2 wheels plus 2 feet) with no gap.
Lid: add a 10-15 mm dome to the top surface, a moulded grab lip along the front edge that overhangs about 30 mm, and make the lid about 35 mm thick at the edge.
Wheels: 200 mm diameter, 50 mm wide, with 8-12 tread blocks on the tyre ring (normal map is fine) and a separate grey hub. Replace the boxy axle housing with a cylindrical axle tube.

Material: lift the albedo to about 0.08-0.10 linear and use roughness 0.55-0.7 with a subtle noise. Add a shared 512 px grime/wear mask: lighter scuffs on the lower front and the lid lip, dark grime streaks below the lid hinge, and UV chalking on the lid top. Vary the tint per instance (green, black, blue, brown council colours).
Optional: add a raised '240L' and a recycling symbol moulded into the side (normal map), and a strip of tape or a sticker remnant, for close-up shots.
renderer_notes: The black lower body in the side view is partly the lack of sky bounce on a dark albedo.

summary: A recognisable moulded bucket seat with a seat number and rear ribs, but the shell drapes like soft material at the front lip, the mounting is generic and the plastic is a flat uniform red.
critique: In the side view the front of the seat pan curls downward and pinches into a droopy, crumpled lip that looks melted. Real stadium bucket seats have a firm, rolled front edge of uniform radius (about 15-25 mm) and a shell of constant 4-6 mm thickness. The back is thin and nearly planar, with a sharp, uneven top edge. The rib grid on the rear of the backrest is a few crossing bars that do not follow the shell curvature. Real seats have an integrated perimeter flange plus 2-4 vertical ribs that merge into the seat pan. The single round pedestal post with bolts scattered on the ground and no base plate reads as wrong: either there is a floor plate with four bolts, or (more typically in UK stands) the seat bolts to a riser bracket or a beam rail. The bolts appear to float. Seat height looks plausible (about 450 mm), but the back top is lower and the back more upright than the 850-900 mm target. The plastic is a single saturated red with a soft highlight. There is no texture grain, no faded or UV-chalked top surfaces, no scuffs on the front lip and no drain holes in the right place (the two black dots look like decals). The number plate is good.
suggestions: Fix the seat-pan front: model it as a single extruded profile curve (back, seat, front roll) with a constant rolled radius of 20 mm and a 5 mm shell thickness. Remove the downward pinch and droop. About 300-500 triangles for the whole shell is enough.

Raise the back top to 850-880 mm above the floor and tilt it back 12-15 degrees. Give the top edge a rolled lip like the front. Add a gentle lumbar double curve to the backrest when seen from the side.

Rear: replace the floating grid with a continuous perimeter flange (15 mm deep) and 3 vertical ribs that run into the seat pan underside. Add moulded mounting bosses under the pan where the bracket attaches.

Mounting: offer two variants. (a) Riser-mounted: a steel L-bracket bolted to the riser face with 2 bolts. (b) Pedestal: a 150 x 150 x 8 mm base plate with 4 hex-head bolts actually seated on the plate. Galvanised grey (albedo about 0.45, metallic, roughness 0.5) rather than black.

Material: drop the red to about (0.45, 0.04, 0.04) linear and use roughness 0.45-0.55 with a fine moulded-texture normal. Add a shared wear mask with lighter UV-faded top surfaces and scuffs on the front lip and back top. Move the drain holes to the lowest point of the pan as true through-holes (two small cylinders).
Make the seat-number plate a slightly proud aluminium plaque (2 mm) with a bevelled edge.

summary: Well-dressed UK fire point with good extinguishers and legible signage, let down by a paper-thin plain back panel, a crumpled canopy and uniform new red paint.
critique: The front is the strong side. The FIRE POINT header, the Fire Action notice, the FOAM/CO2 ID signs, the call point and the two extinguishers (with hose, horn, labels and safety pins) are all convincing and correctly coloured (cream band for foam, black band for CO2). The side view shows that the board is a single thin slab only a few cm thick, with no frame or box section. Real fire point stands are either a folded-steel box section (40-60 mm deep) or a board on two posts, with visible return edges and fixings. The canopy is a curved hood whose front edge folds over itself and kinks in the side view, which reads as a modelling glitch. The back is a flat red rectangle with a faint embossed word and nothing else: no frame, stiffeners or bolts. Extinguisher bases sit in round rings, which is good, but there are no retaining straps or brackets on the board (they look as if they are leaning). The paint is one clean red everywhere (board, base and canopy) with only a speck of wear, and real outdoor units fade to pinkish-orange on top surfaces, chip at edges and get grime at the base. The base plate edge looks a little too thick for a steel plate and too thin for a plinth.
suggestions: Make the board a box section: 50 mm deep with rounded 5 mm bevels, a folded return lip on all edges, and a plain steel back with 2 horizontal stiffening channels and 4-6 visible bolt heads. This adds roughly 200 triangles.

Rebuild the canopy as a clean single-curve sheet (constant radius, 2-3 mm thick, with a folded drip edge at the front) that is attached to the board with 2 side gussets. Remove the self-folding front edge.
Add a wall bracket or strap clip for each extinguisher at about 2/3 height. The handles should hang from hooks so the cylinders stand vertically.

Paint: split the reds. Board albedo about (0.5, 0.05, 0.04), canopy top faded about 15% lighter and more orange, base plate darker with grime and grey chipping at the edges and corners. Use a shared 512 px edge-wear mask.
Base: either a thin 10 mm galvanised plate with 4 anchor bolts, or a 100 mm concrete plinth. Choose one and make it read that way.
Small extras for close-ups: a laminated 'inspection' tag on one extinguisher neck, and a 'CHECKED' sticker that is fully readable (it is currently clipped by the extinguisher).

summary: Reads as a car-park barrier from a distance, but the housing is a plain yellow box, the boom is a thin generic tube and the rest post is just a striped stick.
critique: The layout is right (cabinet on a concrete plinth, boom with red/white bands, a rest post at the far end) and the length is plausible at about 4 m. The detail is far below a real FAAC/CAME unit. The cabinet is a plain rectangular box with rounded top corners and one tiny warning sticker. Real units have a domed or sloped cap, an inspection door with a lock, a visible spring or balance housing, louvres, and often an integrated LED traffic light or flashing beacon. The FAAC 620 reference is 350 x 170 mm in plan and 1080 mm tall. This housing is about right in height but too deep relative to its width and too smooth. The boom attaches by a small flat plate, where a real one uses a chunky cast-aluminium boom holder clamped around the boom end with 4 bolts and a pivot hub on the cabinet side. The boom is a thin round section. Real booms are elliptical or rectangular aluminium profiles about 90 x 50 mm, with a rubber anti-impact strip along the underside and red reflective bands (not flat red paint). The rest post is a bare striped pole sunk into the grass with no Y-fork or cradle for the boom to sit in. Here the boom lies on top of the post with a small dark stub. Materials are clean and uniform: the yellow cabinet has no weathering and the concrete plinth is pristine.
suggestions: Cabinet: 350 W x 300 D x 1080 H steel box (lower the depth) with a sloped or domed top cap that overhangs 20 mm. Add a front door inset 3 mm with a lock barrel, a vent louvre panel, and a hub boss on the boom side (Ø 120 mm, 60 mm proud). This adds roughly 300 triangles.
Boom holder: a cast bracket about 250 mm long that wraps the boom end, with 4 bolt heads and a dark grey metallic finish. It should sit on the hub so the pivot point is obvious.

Boom: change the section to an elliptical or rounded-rectangle profile (90 x 50 mm, 8-12 segments). Add a black rubber strip (25 mm) along the underside. Use red reflective bands with a slightly higher specular than the white paint. Add a thin LED strip line optionally.
Rest post: a 60 mm galvanised post, 900 mm tall, on a small base plate (not sunk into turf), topped with a Y-fork or rubber-lined cradle that the boom sits inside.

Material: yellow albedo about (0.6, 0.42, 0.05) with roughness 0.5. Add a light dust and grime mask on the lower 30% and on the cap edges. Weather the concrete plinth with darker edges and a bolt-down plate. Add a small brand-free nameplate and a warning triangle.
Optional variant: a raised boom pose (85-90 degrees) for open gates, sharing the same mesh.

summary: A convincing small modular security kiosk (door, service window, AC unit, gutter, downpipe, flood light, CCTV, signage) with good interior cards, but the cladding is flat and clean and the hut has no believable ground contact.
critique: The best asset in this batch for its parts list. The flat membrane roof with an overhanging fascia and a gutter, the downpipe, the AC condenser with its pipe run, the bulkhead light, the CCTV dome, the SECURITY sign, the door with a vision panel and kick plate, and the sliding service window with a desk and monitor inside all read correctly. Shortfalls: (1) The wall cladding is a near-white flat material with faint vertical lines. Real GRP or steel-panel kiosks show panel joints with cover strips every 1-1.2 m, visible fixings, slight panel bowing, and staining and green algae streaks below the roof edge and window sills. (2) The base floats. There is a dark recessed band at the bottom but no skid frame, plinth or concrete pad edge (except the step), and the base edge is a perfectly clean line. (3) The windows have frames but no sills, drip edges or rubber gaskets, and the interior cards are flat images with no parallax. (4) The roof membrane colour is a uniform dark grey with a soft sheen. Real membranes show seam welds, ponding stains and debris. (5) The downpipe ends in mid-air at the base without a shoe or drain. (6) The door has no hinges visible and the handle is minimal.
suggestions: Cladding: add a 1 m panel module with 40 mm cover strips (2 mm proud) and a row of fixings at the top and bottom of each panel, all on a normal map. Lower the albedo to about 0.7 off-white with a subtle tint.
Weathering: a 1K shared grime atlas with dark streaks from the roof edge and window sill corners, green algae near the base, and dirt splash in the bottom 150 mm.
Ground: sit the hut on a 100 mm galvanised skid frame or a concrete pad that extends 200 mm past the walls. Add 4 lifting eyes or forklift pockets at the base for the modular read.
Windows: add pressed-steel sills that project 30 mm with a drip edge, and black gaskets. Use a parallax interior-mapping shader (or a 2-layer card) for the service window, which is the hero detail.
Downpipe: add a shoe at the bottom turned out 100 mm over a small gully grate. Add 2 more brackets.
Door: 3 visible hinges, a lever handle with a backplate and a keyhole, a closer arm at the top. Add a key-safe or intercom box beside the door.

summary: A correctly proportioned 205 L drum with rolling hoops, bungs and good labels, but the rust is a flat, saturated, pixelated orange decal applied evenly to every hoop, and the drum is undented.
critique: The size and form are right (about 585 mm diameter x 880 mm high, two rolling hoops, top chime, 2 bungs) and the WASTE OIL stencil, the class 3 diamond and the torn hydraulic-oil label are good storytelling. The wear is what lets it down. The rust is the same bright orange-terracotta everywhere, with jagged pixel-stair edges visible in the close-up. It is applied in an almost even dashed pattern along every hoop and the top and bottom chimes, which looks procedural rather than earned. Real drum wear progresses from scratches and chipped paint showing grey-black bare steel, to dark brown oxidised steel, to flaky orange only in the worst spots. It also concentrates on the bottom chime (where the drum is dragged and stands in water) and the top chime (where it is opened), and less on the hoops. The paint itself is a fresh, uniform saturated blue with even sheen. There are no oil drips or runs from the bungs, no dust or grime on the lid, and no dents or flattened hoops. The surface is a perfect cylinder. There is no visible seam weld line down the side. Some rust on the vertical faces is long thin streak-like spots that look like stretched texture.
suggestions: Wear mask: replace the decal-like rust with a layered mask driven by curvature, height and noise. Layer 1 is chipped paint showing grey steel (albedo about 0.25, metallic 1, roughness 0.5). Layer 2 is dark brown rust (0.12, 0.06, 0.03, roughness 0.9) on the bottom 80 mm and the chime edges. Layer 3 is a small amount of bright orange only at the centres of the worst patches. Use smooth or bilinear edges with noise, not pixel steps. A single shared 1K mask works across instances by randomising the UV offset.
Concentrate wear: bottom chime heavily, top chime moderately, hoops lightly with scuffs rather than rust dashes. Add vertical rust or grime runs below the bungs and the top chime.

Geometry: add 2-4 random soft dents per instance by displacing body vertices (about 32 radial segments x 12 rings is enough). Slightly flatten one section of a hoop. Add a 3 mm side seam weld line. This adds roughly 100 triangles.
Paint: desaturate the blue about 20%, add a faded and chalky top band and a sheen variation (roughness 0.35-0.6 noise). Add per-instance colour variants (blue, red, black, green, galvanised).
Lid: add an oily sheen or dust layer, darker stains around the bungs and a puddle decal option on the ground.

summary: The main building and entrance pavilion are flat-shaded boxes with painted-on windows. The pavilion clips into the main facade and hides the club lettering.
critique: In the main-building view, the timber-clad block is one flat orange-tan plane with fine vertical lines. The windows are dark rectangles with thin brown frames almost flush to the wall (no reveals, sills or heads), and the white rectangles in the upper panes read as random blinds that look like missing textures. There is no plinth, parapet, coping, rainwater goods, entrance canopy, signage zone or lighting. The dark-navy two-storey pavilion in front is a plain box with one cyan stripe, flush grey window frames and a flat double door. It is pushed right against the main facade so that it overlaps windows behind it and covers the 'UNITED' lettering, which is half-hidden and cut by the roofline. That is a layout bug. Real Premier League training centres (e.g. modern Category 1 academies) are sleek, with deep curtain-wall glazing with mullions and reflections, brise-soleil, a large cantilevered entrance canopy, landscaped approach and crest signage. None of that reads. Glass has no reflectivity: it is a matte navy fill. The paving is a clean tiled texture with no kerbs, planters or bollards. From the aerial view, the buildings are small low boxes with green roofs, without a clear hierarchy.
suggestions: Fix placement first: keep a clear 3-6 m gap between the pavilion and the main block (or join them properly as one massing with a shared roofline), and place the club lettering on a free wall or a canopy fascia where nothing can occlude it.

Windows: recess the glass 150-200 mm behind the wall plane with real reveal geometry. Add a 50 mm proud sill and a head flashing. Use a glass material with low roughness (0.05), a slight blue-grey albedo and environment reflection, or a cheap cube-map, instead of matte navy. Remove the random white 'blind' quads, or make them consistent half-drawn blinds behind the glass.

Facade: give the timber cladding board-width variation and tonal noise (shared 1K tileable texture with a normal map), plus a 300-500 mm dark brick or concrete plinth, a metal coping on the parapet and downpipes every 8-10 m.

Entrance: add a cantilevered canopy (about 2.5 m deep) with recessed downlights, full-height glazed doors with mullions and a crest or name sign on a dedicated totem or fascia. Add bollards, planters and cycle stands from the existing kit along the frontage.
Pavilion: replace the flat navy with a composite-panel facade (1.2 x 0.6 m joints) or full curtain wall. Add a roof parapet with plant equipment and louvres to break the box.
Aerial read: vary roof heights and add rooftop plant, solar panels and roof-light grids so the buildings read as buildings from above.
renderer_notes: The lack of reflections (no SSR/probes) makes all glass look dead. A single blurred sky cubemap for glass would help every building in the kit.

summary: The cars and solar canopies are reasonable individually, but trees grow through the canopy, a canopy column passes through a car, and the parking layout shows duplicated plates and cars overlapping bays.
critique: This view has hard collision bugs that break realism immediately. (1) Birch trunks rise straight through the solar canopy roof in several places. (2) A canopy column passes through the roof of the grey saloon in the second row, and other cars sit on the column footings. (3) Cars are not centred in bays: several straddle lines or overlap the next bay. (4) Registration plates repeat (LR70 HNF and KD19 RVX on several cars in one view). (5) The asphalt is a uniform dark navy with no texture, no oil stains, tyre marks, patching or drainage gullies. There are no kerbs, so the tarmac meets the grass at a hard edge. Bay lines are crisp and unworn. (6) The canopy is a thin flat plane on round posts, missing the steel purlins, the inverter boxes and the tilted panel rows. The vehicles themselves are decent at mid-distance: correct body styles, light bars, plates, wheels and varied colours. Up close, the glass is opaque grey-black, the panel gaps are faint and the tyres sit slightly into the ground. The landscape planting between the rows is just grass with no kerb or edging.
suggestions: Collision rules: treat canopy footprints (posts and roof outline plus 0.5 m) as exclusion zones for tree placement, and treat each bay rectangle as the only legal footprint for a car. Snap each car to the bay centre with a small random offset (+/-0.15 m) and yaw (+/-3 degrees). Leave 10-20% of bays empty.
Plates: generate a unique plate per instance from the seed (UK format: 2 letters, 2 digits, space, 3 letters), front white and rear yellow.

Asphalt: use a tileable 1K asphalt albedo and normal (mid-grey, about 0.12-0.15 linear, not navy) plus a decal layer of oil stains under the middle of each bay, tyre scuffs and a few patched rectangles. Fade the white lines with wear at the bay mouths.
Edges: add 125 mm precast kerbs around islands and the car-park perimeter, with dropped kerbs at pedestrian routes. Add gully grates every 15-20 m.

Solar canopy: add a steel I-beam spine and purlins under the panels, angle the panel field 5-10 degrees, show panel-module gaps and add 1-2 inverter boxes and cable trays on the posts. Add EV chargers at a row end.

Cars: make the glass slightly reflective and lighter (albedo 0.05, roughness 0.05 with a sky cubemap) so interiors and reflections hint through, and ensure the tyres have a flattened contact patch rather than sinking.

summary: Credible training pitches with correct markings, floodlights, fencing, goals, mannequins, poles, cones, dugout and filming tower, but the grass is a flat-shaded colour field and the kit is sparse and small in frame.
critique: The layout reads as a professional training centre: multiple full-size pitches separated by ball-stop fencing, floodlight columns, mini and full goals, a yellow mannequin wall, slalom poles, cones, a team shelter and a filming scaffold tower. The line markings are crisp and correctly drawn. Weaknesses: (1) The grass is a flat gradient with soft broad mow stripes and no blade texture, wear or colour variation. Real elite training pitches show strong, sharp 4-6 m mow stripes, worn goalmouths and centre circle, darker divots and repair patches. (2) The lines are too perfect and too bright, with no slight width noise or grass bleeding through. (3) The floodlight columns are thin with tiny heads (2 lamps), which looks more like amenity lighting than training-pitch floodlights. They usually carry 4-8 lamps on a cross-arm. (4) The ball-stop netting reads as a faint dotted haze, without visible posts and top rails at the right density. (5) Training kit is sparse for a Premier session: a few cones and poles scattered with no deliberate drill layout. (6) Floating 'H' shaped shadows on the pitch come from an off-screen object and look odd. The filming tower and shelter are a good touch.
suggestions: Grass: use a tileable 2K grass albedo with micro variation, plus crisp mow stripes at 5 m (+/-10% value contrast with a sharp transition) in the direction of play. Add wear decals around the goalmouths, the centre circle and corner arcs (browner, about 15% darker), and a few divot decals.
Lines: give them 120 mm width with slight noise on the edges and about 10% grass showing through, and an albedo of about 0.8, not 1.0.
Floodlights: a 15-18 m column with a cross-arm carrying 4-6 rectangular LED floods tilted down. Add a base door and a concrete base.
Fencing: model posts every 3 m with a top rail, and ball-stop net as a tileable alpha with a 40-50 mm mesh. Make it visibly darker green or black at mid-distance.

Drills: place training kit as recognisable drill sets (rondo squares with 4 cones, an agility ladder plus pole slalom, a mannequin wall at 9.15 m from a ball line, mini goals at both ends of a small-sided area), plus a ball cart, bibs on the fence and water-bottle carriers.
Check what is casting the floating 'H' shadows and either make the caster visible or remove it.

summary: A logical site plan (access road, boundary, pitches, buildings, car park, tree belts) set in a patchwork of fields, but the surrounding countryside is a flat colour quilt with lollipop trees and no hedgerows, so it reads like a strategy-game map.
critique: From the air, the site makes sense: a private access road off the lane, a perimeter fence, a cluster of buildings with the car park next to them, a row of pitches with an indoor hall, a construction or maintenance yard, and tree lines. The scale relationships look plausible. The countryside around it is the weak part. The fields are flat-coloured polygons in a few tones of green, yellow and brown, with no crop rows, tramlines or texture, and no field-edge hedgerows (only thin dark lines). They tile in a near-regular grid with a few curved boundaries, so the repetition is obvious. Trees are isolated identical round clumps placed in single lines with even spacing. Real English countryside has thick, continuous hedgerows with occasional standard oaks, copses and woodland blocks, farm buildings, ditches and lanes with verges. The main grass inside the site shows a blotchy camouflage noise at large scale. The access road is a uniform grey strip with no verges, markings or junction mouth. The site boundary has no visible fence, gatehouse or entrance feature at this scale, and there are no paths between the buildings and the pitches. Distant fields fade into haze, which helps.
suggestions: Hedgerows: extrude a cheap hedge strip (cards or a low mesh, 1.5-2.5 m H, 1-2 m W) along every field boundary, with a standard tree every 30-80 m. This single change will make the landscape read as English.

Fields: give each field a tileable crop texture (wheat rows, ploughed furrows, pasture, oilseed yellow in season) aligned to the longest edge, with tramlines every 24 m and a darker headland strip around the edge.
Trees: cluster trees into copses and woodland blocks with 5-6 species mixes and size variation (0.6-1.4x). Avoid single evenly-spaced rows except along the drive, where an avenue makes sense.
Large-scale grass: replace the camouflage blotch with a lower-contrast, multi-octave noise blended with a macro texture. Keep the variation under 8% value.

Site: add a gatehouse or barrier at the site entrance (the kit already has a security hut and barrier arm), perimeter weld-mesh fencing with a tree belt inside, footpaths linking the buildings to the pitches, a maintenance compound and a small pond or SuDS basin.
Roads: add verges, white edge lines, a bellmouth junction with the lane and a few passing places on the lane.
renderer_notes: The haze and lack of large-scale shadowing (no AO from hedgerows or woods) flattens the aerial view. Part of the low score is lighting, but the missing hedgerows are an asset problem.
